articles.headline: El Gobierno deja a Lugo sin el 2% Cultural para el Museo da Romanización
articles.subtitle: La propuesta de resolución excluye el proyecto lucense, de 15,2 millones, de las 78 actuaciones financiadas en toda España. El Concello había reservado 3,8 millones propios y tenía el aval de Patrimonio.
articles.body:
El Ministerio de Vivienda y Agenda Urbana no incluirá el proyecto lucense entre las 78 actuaciones que recibirán financiación del 2% Cultural. La propuesta de resolución provisional de la convocatoria, firmada este martes por la directora general de Agenda Urbana y Arquitectura, deja fuera la conversión del antiguo cuartel de San Fernando en Museo da Romanización, un plan valorado en 15,2 millones de euros.

El Concello había pedido 11,4 millones al programa estatal y había comprometido 3.800.308 euros de fondos propios, ya reservados en el crédito de los últimos presupuestos municipales. El expediente parecía encaminado: Patrimonio Cultural de la Xunta emitió un informe favorable y el Ministerio cerró a finales de julio la preevaluación documental.

## El coste, la hipótesis más probable

Ni la resolución ni su anexo explican por qué no figura Lugo, de modo que no consta si fue descartado por motivos formales o por quedarse por debajo de la puntuación de corte. Las solicitudes admitidas suman 133 millones frente a los 80 que reparte el programa.

La comparación apunta al tamaño de la petición. La actuación más beneficiada, el monasterio de las Madres Dominicas de Santa Catalina de Siena de Valladolid, recibe 4,22 millones, casi un tercio de lo que solicitaba la ciudad. El Concello sostiene que dio los pasos correctos y reclamará explicaciones al Ministerio.

articles.headline: Lugo mantendrá su ZBE sin multas hasta 2027 pese al endurecimiento del decreto
articles.subtitle: El decreto suprime las moratorias y exige sanciones reales, mientras la ciudad conserva su periodo de gracia hasta septiembre de 2027 con 28 cámaras ya instaladas.
articles.body:
El Consejo de Ministros aprobó este martes la modificación del Real Decreto 1052/2022 para garantizar que las Zonas de Bajas Emisiones funcionen de verdad. La norma obliga a las entidades locales a acreditar documentalmente el cumplimiento de los requisitos, a comunicar la entrada en vigor de las prohibiciones de acceso y estacionamiento y a aplicar un régimen sancionador efectivo, sin periodos transitorios.

El Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica justifica el cambio en las deficiencias detectadas desde 2023: moratorias prolongadas, zonas declaradas sin restricciones reales de acceso y perímetros que coincidían con espacios ya limitados al tráfico.

## Lugo, en periodo de prueba

Lugo activó su Zona de Bajas Emisiones el 17 de septiembre dentro de un periodo de adaptación de doce meses, que se extiende hasta el 18 de septiembre de 2027 y durante el cual no se impondrán sanciones. La ordenanza reorganiza la circulación en el casco histórico.

Los residentes, los comerciantes y los propietarios de plazas de garaje acceden al recinto con un registro previo, sin límite de vehículos por persona y con renovación solo si cambia el coche. También pueden entrar quienes van a un aparcamiento y la seguridad privada en servicio.

Las personas con movilidad reducida o con acompañamiento acreditado, los profesionales, las mudanzas y los vehículos hoteleros necesitan una comunicación previa. Si no la presentaron y reciben una multa, disponen de cinco días para justificarla. El Concello instaló 18 equipos de lectura de matrículas y diez cámaras de vigilancia de peatones y ciclistas en los accesos al recinto.

articles.headline: Óscar Puente dimite como ministro y renuncia a ser candidato del PSOE el 29-N
articles.subtitle: El ministro deja el cargo y también su escaño y la candidatura socialista, seis días después del siniestro de Urda y tras una semana de presiones internas.
articles.body:
Óscar Puente dimitió este martes como ministro de Transportes casi a las diez de la noche, al término de una comparecencia de casi cinco horas ante la Diputación Permanente del Congreso. También renunció a ser candidato del PSOE y diputado por la lista del 29-N, seis días después del accidente ferroviario de Urda, que ha dejado 69 muertos.

El ya exministro aseguró, visiblemente emocionado, que la decisión estaba tomada desde la mañana del propio siniestro, el 28 de octubre, cuando se dirigía al centro de control de Adif. «Un ministro de transportes de un país como España no puede continuar en su cargo con dos accidentes de esta gravedad en un año», dijo.

## Una semana de presiones

Su salida cierra siete días en los que Moncloa alternó respaldos públicos y presiones internas para que dejara el cargo antes del miércoles. Pedro Sánchez había calificado el siniestro de «inasumible» nueve meses después del de Adamuz, donde murieron 46 personas, y prometió actuar «con contundencia».

El presidente del Gobierno reaccionó a la dimisión con un mensaje de agradecimiento: «Ha dado la cara. Por voluntad propia. Gracias por tanto, compañero». El mismo Consejo de Ministros aprobó ayudas de 30 millones para los afectados por el accidente.

La renuncia deja al PSOE sin uno de sus perfiles más reconocibles a cuatro semanas de las elecciones generales y traslada la gestión de la crisis ferroviaria a quien ocupe la cartera en un Gobierno en funciones.

articles.headline: El Gobierno exige un segundo controlador y recorta trenes mientras llega el ERTMS
articles.subtitle: El paquete aprobado tras Urda introduce inteligencia artificial en la supervisión y reduce frecuencias en Madrid-Sevilla hasta que se complete la nueva señalización.
articles.body:
El Consejo de Ministros aprobó este martes un plan para reforzar la seguridad de la alta velocidad, seis días después del choque de Urda. Las decisiones que se tomen en los centros de control cuando no funcionen los sistemas automáticos de bloqueo deberán ser supervisadas y validadas por un segundo controlador humano.

El plan añade un nuevo software para los centros de control, con alertas automáticas, registro electrónico de telefonemas, listas de verificación y una ergonomía visual que permita localizar mejor los trenes y el estado de las vías. También se usará inteligencia artificial para vigilar el funcionamiento del sistema y anticipar escenarios anómalos.

## Menos trenes mientras se instala el ERTMS

Se completará el despliegue del ERTMS nivel 2 en la línea Madrid-Sevilla y la Agencia Estatal de Seguridad Ferroviaria hará una auditoría «extraordinaria e inmediata» de sus sistemas, que actualizará la de noviembre de 2025. Hasta que ambos trabajos terminen, algo previsto para comienzos de 2027, se reducirá la frecuencia de trenes en ese corredor.

Un estudio con expertos independientes evaluará además medidas de seguridad pasiva en los vagones, como convertir los espacios de equipajes en compartimentos cerrados que eviten proyecciones en frenazos bruscos o impactos.

Puente defendió la seguridad del sistema español, que los organismos internacionales sitúan entre los mejores del mundo, pero admitió la «imperiosa necesidad de reforzar» un modelo que acumula 115 muertos en menos de un año: 69 en Urda y 46 en Adamuz.

articles.headline: Los sindicatos rechazan la petición de Feijóo de aplazar la huelga del 11-N
articles.subtitle: UGT y CCOO responden que la tragedia de Urda añade motivos a la protesta por la vivienda, mientras la patronal respalda al líder del PP.
articles.body:
UGT y CCOO rechazaron este lunes la petición de Alberto Núñez Feijóo de desconvocar la huelga general del 11 de noviembre por la vivienda. El líder del PP había afirmado en un desayuno informativo que, tras la tragedia de Urda, mantener los paros era «un grave error» y un «problema reputacional» para los sindicatos.

«Uno de los motivos de la huelga es precisamente reivindicar la inversión en los servicios públicos y el sostenimiento de las grandes infraestructuras», respondió el secretario general de CCOO, Unai Sordo. A su juicio, el accidente añade razones a la protesta en lugar de restarlas.

## «No es contra la oposición»

Sordo negó que la convocatoria vaya dirigida contra el PP, aunque recordó que los populares votaron en contra de convalidar los decretos de vivienda, de modo que «podrá ser apelado como poder legislativo». El Sindicato de Inquilinas confirmó que mantiene los paros.

La Confederación Española de Organizaciones Empresariales respaldó a Feijóo. Su presidente, Antonio Garamendi, valoró «muy positivamente» la petición de desconvocatoria y sostuvo que lo urgente es «ponerse a trabajar para arreglar los trenes».

El pulso llega a cuatro semanas de las elecciones del 29-N y convierte la huelga en un test de fuerza entre sindicatos, Gobierno y oposición sobre quién capitaliza el malestar por el precio de la vivienda.

articles.headline: Martin sets up State study of a united Ireland's three possible shapes
articles.subtitle: The Taoiseach's Futures Study Initiative will test a unitary republic, a devolved all-island state and the status quo, and invites unionists to take part.
articles.body:
The Taoiseach, Micheál Martin, is to establish a State-funded study of what a united Ireland would actually involve, telling his parliamentary party on Tuesday that the debate has to move from assertion to evidence.

The Futures Study Initiative will examine three scenarios: a single unitary republic run from Dublin and fully in place within five years of a border poll, with no devolved administration in Belfast; an all-island state that keeps a devolved government along the lines of the current one; and the continuation of the Good Friday Agreement settlement without constitutional change.

It will not recommend any of them. Instead a chairperson and at least five members, advised by specialists, will map what each would require across constitutional and legal change, the economy, health, education, security, and symbols and culture, then publish a report for the Irish government.

## An invitation to unionists

The policy paper says the process offers a "good faith opportunity for those outside the nationalist tradition to participate" and would "challenge all traditions to move from making general assertions about the future to engaging with hard evidence". Every party and campaign group will be invited to make submissions.

Martin has been careful to say the work does not interfere with or seek to replace existing North-South and British-Irish commitments. A dedicated secretariat would sit in his own department.

The move comes days before Fine Gael, his coalition partner, publishes its own unity blueprint at its conference in Cork this weekend, and with opposition parties pressing Dublin to prepare for a border poll.

articles.headline: Democrats take both chambers of Congress as Trump's candidates fall
articles.subtitle: Annie Andrews, a paediatrician, unseated the president's hand-picked candidate in a state he won by 18 points, as Democrats flipped four Senate seats and held Georgia.
articles.body:
Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, turning a midterm election fought over the cost of living and the war with Iran into a broad repudiation of Donald Trump. The party flipped Senate seats in South Carolina, North Carolina, Texas and Iowa, and held Georgia and New Hampshire.

The most striking result came in South Carolina, where Annie Andrews, a paediatrician, beat Darline Graham, the president's hand-picked candidate, in a state he carried by almost 18 points two years ago. She is the first Democrat to win a Senate seat there in 28 years.

## A wave that reached deep Republican ground

Graham, the sister of the late senator Lindsey Graham, had been appointed to the seat and was encouraged by Trump to run for a full term. Her inexperience proved a liability. In Florida, Republican senator Ashley Moody held on against Angie Nixon but by only about three points, in a state Trump won by 13 in 2024.

Jon Ossoff, who held his Georgia seat, told supporters the result was a rebuke of the president's "depravity, corruption and incompetence". In Ohio, Sherrod Brown won a return to the Senate, while Amy Acton defeated Vivek Ramaswamy in the governor's race.

Control of the chamber hands Democrats subpoena power over the administration and the ability to block appointments. Trump attributed the losses to his absence from the ballot, saying Republicans would have swept had he been running.

articles.headline: Bomb threats force emergency landings on flights across Europe
articles.subtitle: A Heathrow flight diverted to Warsaw and a Ryanair service from Manchester was searched in Murcia, after a week of hoaxes that has unsettled European aviation.
articles.body:
Three passenger aircraft were searched after landing in Poland and Spain on Tuesday following bomb threats, the latest in a series of alerts that have disrupted European aviation over the past week.

A flight from London Heathrow to Warsaw made an unscheduled landing at Modlin airport, north of the Polish capital, with 181 people on board. The Boeing 737 Max touched down shortly after 10:00 local time and passengers were taken off while specialists inspected the aircraft. A second flight, from Copenhagen to Warsaw's Chopin airport, also received a threat but landed normally.

In Spain, a Ryanair flight from Manchester to Murcia was inspected on arrival, with 121 passengers and crew aboard, according to Francisco Lucas, the central government's delegate in the region. Fire crews were mobilised at Murcia-Corvera airport as a precaution.

## How many flights, and who is behind it

Accounts of the scale differed. Al Jazeera and Sky News reported seven flights affected across Europe, while Ireland's RTÉ said two Ryanair flights from Dublin had also been searched. No device has been found in any of the aircraft checked so far.

The alerts follow Monday's emergency landing in Budapest of a Wizz Air flight from London Luton, which was escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet. The airline said afterwards that checks had found nothing. Polish authorities said normal operations at Modlin had resumed.

articles.headline: Iran warns nobody gains from war as Trump confirms new strikes
articles.subtitle: The US president confirmed an attack on Qeshm Island and called it minor, while Tehran said it was ready for battle and Qatar kept pushing for an interim deal.
articles.body:
Iran warned on Wednesday that no one would benefit from a return to war, hours after Donald Trump confirmed that American aircraft had struck a target on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The president described the raid as a minor attack on an anti-aircraft facility that had just been completed.

Trump told Fox News that the United States was "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it", and told the Financial Times that Washington seemed to be "getting everything we want". Iran's chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the republic was "ready for battle with its finger on the trigger", while the deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, insisted Tehran retained the right to self-defence.

## Mediators still talking

President Masoud Pezeshkian struck a softer note, saying his government was still pursuing a settlement "through dialogue" and that nobody would gain if the war reignited. He noted that the supreme leader had recently given the government powers to negotiate matters previously considered off-limits.

Qatar, which has been shuttling proposals between the two sides, said both were reviewing them and that it remained hopeful of an interim deal. Israel's military said it was not involved in the latest strikes.

The Revolutionary Guards said four oil tankers had been destroyed by mines in the strait and two other vessels halted, a claim that could not be independently verified. Brent crude fell more than 3% to about $101 a barrel as traders bet against a wider escalation.

articles.headline: Trump says US will cut off $4bn a year in military aid to Israel
articles.subtitle: The president said the annual package would stop at the end of the year without giving details, and Israeli officials said they had not been told of any such agreement.
articles.body:
Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he had agreed with Benjamin Netanyahu to end the roughly $4bn in military aid the United States sends Israel each year, telling Fox News the money would be "cut off at the end of the year".

"Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," the president said in a phone interview. He gave no details, and a spokesman for the Israeli prime minister said he knew nothing of the remark but would check.

Trump argued that Israel was fine with it because it had "become a very successful country", adding: "We won't be paying any more Israel." He called the arrangement "a wasted thing".

## Two numbers, one announcement

The exact figure is disputed. NBC News reported $4bn, while Al Jazeera put the annual package at $3.8bn, the sum set out in the ten-year aid memorandum signed in 2016. Neither the State Department nor the Israeli government confirmed any change.

Oil prices slid on the comments, with Brent crude down more than 3% to around $101 a barrel, its lowest in more than three weeks. Traders read the remark, alongside the president's suggestion that he would not attack Iran again, as a sign the war might be winding down.

US aid to Israel and the war in Gaza were among the most contentious issues of the midterm campaign, and the announcement came as results were still being counted.

articles.headline: Two helicopters collide near Everest base camp, killing Indian trekker
articles.subtitle: The aircraft came down at Pheriche while ferrying hikers off the mountain, in the second emergency on the Everest route this week.
articles.body:
Two helicopters collided while trying to land near Everest base camp on Tuesday, killing an Indian trekker and injuring two other people in the latest accident on Nepal's busiest mountain route.

The aircraft came down at Pheriche, a village at 13,780 feet where trekkers acclimatise, according to Bhupendra Thapa of the Solukhumbu district administration. The dead man was 47. A passenger from New Zealand was flown to Kathmandu for treatment, and the Nepali pilot was treated locally.

Both helicopters were ferrying hikers down from the base camp trek during Nepal's autumn season, the window between the monsoon and the hard winter. There are no roads on the approach, so helicopters are the only way to evacuate people who fall ill or are exhausted by the altitude.

## A bad week on the trail

It was the second emergency on the route in days. On Friday a fire broke out at a hotel in Dingboche, about two miles from Pheriche, possibly started by a cooking gas cylinder. Guests and staff were evacuated and nobody was hurt.

Heavy snow had closed the trail earlier in the week before the weather cleared on Sunday, releasing thousands of trekkers who had been waiting for the route to reopen. The number of people aboard the two helicopters has not been confirmed.

articles.headline: The memory crunch reaches the shelf: iPhones, PCs and graphics cards all cost more
articles.subtitle: Apple's margin forecast missed as its component bill rose $33bn in a quarter, and Nvidia is raising RTX prices again. The cause is data centres buying up every chip.
articles.body:
Apple's first earnings report under John Ternus ended with the number investors cared about most: a forecast gross margin of 45% to 46% for the December quarter, below the 46.3% analysts expected. The cause was memory. "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," Ternus told analysts on Monday.

Apple's purchase obligations rose $33bn between the June and September quarters as it raced to lock in supply, and the company said it expects shortages of iPhones and Macs through Christmas. It has already raised prices on Macs and iPads at the end of June and added $100 to every iPhone in September.

## Everyone is paying

Nvidia is passing the cost on too. This week it told buyers that RTX 50-series graphics cards are going up again, with the RTX 5090 rising by $500 and the RTX 5050 by $30 to $50. AMD and Intel have not moved yet.

The root cause is data centres. Nvidia and the hyperscalers are buying every DRAM and NAND chip they can find and paying a premium for it, leaving consumer manufacturers to compete for whatever is left. SK Hynix has said the shortage could last until 2030, and Intel does not expect relief next year.

Microsoft's answer is software: it says Windows 11 is now about 20% more responsive and 40% faster at multitasking on machines with only 8GB of RAM, which is what many buyers will be able to afford. AMD chief executive Lisa Su was blunter, saying she is planning on "a down year for 2027" in PCs.

articles.headline: Binance says fake job interviews and a poisoned AI tool let hackers take $6.3bn
articles.subtitle: An engineer was groomed through a fake recruitment process, then the intruders used the exchange's own internal AI tool to reach two more laptops.
articles.body:
Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn from Binance got in through a fake recruitment process and then used one of the company's own AI tools against it, the exchange said in its first detailed account of the breach.

An engineer was approached on a legitimate jobs platform and invited to interviews with people posing as representatives of a real company. To build trust the attackers shared social media profiles carrying personal photographs. At a second interview the engineer was asked to download an "assignment" that was malware, wrapped in obfuscation that got it past security tooling.

## One laptop became three

From that machine the intruders took control of an internal AI tool in October and used it to reach the laptops of two more engineers, giving them the access they needed to drain wallets. Binance suspended withdrawals worldwide while it worked out what had happened; customers pulled billions of dollars out once the service reopened on Sunday.

The company has apologised, says it has set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss and that 98% of affected tokens had been replenished by Saturday. About half of the stolen assets have been frozen, with the FBI and Secret Service helping to trace the rest.

US agencies and private analysts say the attack carries the hallmarks of North Korea. Pyongyang denies it; Kim Yo Jong called the accusation a "sinister attempt" to damage the country's image.

articles.headline: AMD posts the biggest quarter in its history as data centres take over
articles.subtitle: Revenue hit a record $13.4bn on $8.5bn of data centre sales, but gaming fell 40% and Lisa Su is planning for a shrinking PC market next year.
articles.body:
AMD reported record quarterly revenue of $13.4bn for the three months to September, including $8.5bn of data centre sales, and told investors to expect $17bn in the current quarter against a $16.2bn consensus. The shares rose about 7% after hours.

Chief executive Lisa Su called it "the largest and most profitable" quarter in the company's history and said revenue would grow more than 80% in 2027. Chief financial officer Jean Hu went further: beyond 2027, she expects data centres to account for more than 80% of everything AMD sells. They were 63% of revenue last quarter, up from 47% a year earlier.

The driver is not only GPUs. Agentic AI workloads, which run for hours without a human in the loop, lean heavily on server CPUs, and AMD's Epyc line has taken share. Its Helios rack-scale systems now compete directly with Nvidia's, and Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, Anthropic and OpenAI have begun installing them.

## The other half of the business is shrinking

Client and gaming revenue fell 8% to $3.7bn, with gaming down 40% to $773m as memory prices pushed up console and graphics card costs. Su conceded that component costs are slowing consumer sell-through and said AMD is planning for a down PC year in 2027.

The company has also been spending: $8.2bn in stock for World Labs in September, $1bn into Meta's equity offering and a commitment of up to $5bn in Anthropic.

articles.headline: Canva cuts 22% of its staff as growth stalls for the first time in a decade
articles.subtitle: Some 1,271 roles are affected, with some staff losing jobs and others asked to relocate, after the company halved its revenue growth forecast in August.
articles.body:
Canva will shed 1,271 jobs, roughly 22% of its workforce, after the Sydney design-software company's growth slowed for the first time in ten years.

Chief executive Melanie Perkins told staff on Tuesday that some of those affected will lose their roles, others will be asked to relocate to central hubs and others will see their jobs change. She called it "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" and said this had been the company's hardest year yet.

The restructuring folds the product, growth and platform divisions into a single product organisation to cut coordination overhead, concentrates staff in fewer locations, and offers departing employees a US$10,000 grant.

## Growth forecast cut, valuation marked down

The warning signs were already public. In August Canva cut its 2026 revenue growth forecast from 30% to 20%. Its largest institutional backer, Blackbird, marked the company's valuation down 17% to US$34.9bn, citing concern that AI could displace software businesses.

Canva also faces direct competition from image and design models built by OpenAI and Google, which can produce marketing assets that once required a designer and a template library.

The company has not said how many of the 1,271 will actually leave, and the mix matters: a role change or a relocation is a softer outcome than a redundancy, but all of it counts against the headline figure.

articles.headline: Safari gets vertical tabs and a dark mode that fixes websites for you
articles.subtitle: The iOS 27.3 beta moves tabs to a left-hand rail and offers to repaint pages that have no dark design of their own. Developers can opt out.
articles.body:
Apple's iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 betas add a Vertical Tabs layout to Safari, placing the tab strip down the left side of the window. Tabs show as icons by default to save space, with an option to widen the bar so titles appear, and the layout works with Tab Groups and the Topics that Apple Intelligence creates when it sorts tabs automatically.

It is switched on from Safari's settings, or from the View menu on Mac and iPad.

The more interesting addition is Adaptive Dark Mode. If you use Dark Mode and open a site with a bright background, Safari offers a "Try" button. Accept it and the browser renders its own dark version of the page: the background darkens, text contrast is adjusted, logos and graphics are inverted, vector artwork is recoloured, raised surfaces are lifted and layered shadows are rebalanced.

## Not every site, not every tweak

The changes are applied selectively. Apple says each site is adapted according to what it needs to stay readable, so not every adjustment is used everywhere. If a site already has a native dark design, Adaptive Dark Mode does not engage, and developers can add a tag telling Safari to leave their pages as they intended.

Users can turn it on for all sites or keep it per-site after trying it. The same beta round adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look, brings GitHub Copilot into Xcode's built-in coding assistant, and extends Siri's AI features to more languages.

Safari's tab design has been contentious since Apple moved the address bar to the bottom of the iPhone screen. A left-hand tab rail is a bigger change for iPad and Mac than it is for the phone.

articles.headline: Google will switch off Search for schools that refuse its AI tools
articles.subtitle: The policy, reported by the New York Times, drew accusations of extortion from Bernie Sanders and Zohran Mamdani. Google says schools remain in control.
articles.body:
Google is defending a policy that would turn off Search for schools which reject artificial intelligence tools, after a New York Times report on the arrangement triggered a political backlash.

The company's education vice-president, Chris Phillips, told the Times that "Search and AI are deeply integrated", and Google's own statement did not dispute that search access now depends on accepting AI features. In a blog post titled Designing responsible AI for learning, the company said it is bringing a product called Guided Learning into Classroom.

Responding on X, Google said the policy was about giving schools choice: Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search are all off by default, schools stay in control, and AI Mode and AI Overviews will now walk students through problems step by step rather than handing over answers.

## "Extortion"

Critics were not mollified. New York mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google was "trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools". Senator Bernie Sanders called the policy "extortion", saying the company was "threatening schools". Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, said the episode showed "the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service".

The fight lands in the middle of a wider argument about technology in classrooms. Common Sense Media has rated Google's AI overviews an "unacceptable risk" for children, and senators Richard Blumenthal and Josh Hawley opened an inquiry last month into the company's push of AI into schools. Google has already lost antitrust cases over search and advertising.

For schools the practical question is narrow and awkward: search is how students and teachers find material, and Google is now tying it to a product many of them do not want.

articles.headline: Nvidia tells cloud customers to take less Chinese business — and shrugs at open models
articles.subtitle: Cloud providers are being asked to keep Chinese customers under 49% of their book, closing a gap in export controls that let labs rent chips abroad.
articles.body:
Nvidia has begun telling data centre customers to reduce the share of their business that comes from Chinese companies, closing a gap in US export controls that let Chinese AI developers rent American chips abroad without importing them.

The guidance asks cloud providers, including Nvidia-backed start-ups known as neoclouds, to keep Chinese customers to no more than 49% of their book and to disclose who is using the hardware. It is not mandatory, applies only to future contracts, and according to the Financial Times was passed on verbally by sales staff rather than published in a document. Tom's Hardware reports that it applies to data centres worldwide, not just those in Asia.

The target is remote access. Export rules restrict the shipment of chips but say little about renting compute in a data centre in another country, which is how Chinese labs have been reaching top-end Nvidia hardware. US authorities began looking into the practice after allegations involving Moonshot AI, the developer behind the Kimi chatbot.

## Unbothered about who wins the models

Speaking at Fireworks AI's Forge event in San Francisco, Jensen Huang made clear where Nvidia's loyalties lie. "We love closed models," he said, but added that "the idea that all of us would be based on general intelligence is not logical", arguing that most of the world's value sits in specialised models tuned to a particular domain.

His host had a sharper message. Fireworks chief executive Lin Qiao put up a slide of ten headlines about token costs and said: "Cost is out of control. Business cannot scale without borrowing a lot of money."

articles.headline: SUSE cuts one job in ten as Gartner warns the AI redundancies will be reversed
articles.subtitle: The enterprise Linux vendor blamed automation and AI for the losses. Analysts expect 30% of the roles cut for that reason to be rehired by 2029, at a higher cost.
articles.body:
SUSE will cut about one in ten of its nearly 2,000 staff, chief executive Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen told employees, attributing the reduction to automation and AI.

"AI capabilities are advancing exponentially, forcing us to radically reimagine our work," he wrote. "The organizational design and cost base that SUSE is built on today will not carry us forward successfully." The enterprise Linux vendor's decision, first reported by The Register, makes it one of the few European software firms to name AI explicitly as the reason for redundancies. Squarespace also announced job cuts this week, though it has not tied them so directly to AI.

## The bill arrives later

Analyst firm Gartner argues that many of these reductions will be undone. It predicts that 30% of employees laid off because of AI will have been rehired by 2029, typically at a higher cost than before, because companies are cutting roles on the strength of automation business cases that do not survive contact with real workflows.

That warning is appearing in more places. Forrester has said the rush to automate will come back to haunt enterprises, and other analysts argue that some firms are using AI as cover for layoffs they would have made anyway after over-hiring during the boom.

For SUSE's remaining staff the immediate question is what the reorganisation leaves behind. The company has spent years repositioning itself around subscription revenue and containers, and cutting a tenth of the workforce is the largest signal yet of how much slack it believes AI has taken out of the business.

articles.headline: CrowdStrike adds an off switch for AI agents and buys two firms to police them
articles.subtitle: The kill switch terminates a misbehaving agent and cuts its network access. Two acquisitions worth a reported $495m test agents before and after deployment.
articles.body:
CrowdStrike has shipped an AI Kill Switch that lets security teams terminate a misbehaving AI agent, strip its network access and stop it restarting, as companies look for ways to keep autonomous software on a leash.

The feature was announced at the company's Fal.Con Europe conference and sits inside Falcon Guardian, which catalogues the AI agents running inside an organisation and checks them against policy. "Everyone is building AI agents, but they never had the off button, and now they do," chief executive George Kurtz said.

## Half a billion dollars of insurance

Alongside the launch, CrowdStrike said it will acquire two start-ups that secure AI agents, for a reported $495m according to the Wall Street Journal. Fiddler AI, believed to be about four-fifths of that sum, tests agents before deployment by trying model and configuration combinations to find the least risky one, then screens live traffic with a set of custom models called Centor that add under 80 milliseconds of latency.

Dreadnode attacks agents on purpose, running more than 100 breach techniques against them and against the MCP servers they use.

Kurtz compared the kill switch to an airbag: a safeguard that matters precisely because designers cannot guarantee correct behaviour at runtime. He also pointed to CrowdStrike's partnership with Anthropic, claiming enterprise customers told Anthropic they would not deploy its Claude Cowork product without CrowdStrike's protection in place.

The market is responding to a real gap. Agents are being handed credentials, file access and the ability to spend money, and most organisations have no inventory of what is running, let alone a way to stop it.
